title: OPEC October Output Jumps by Nearly 2M Bpd, Global Grid Expansion Surges 50%, and a 125-Fold Yttrium Price Gap Looms Over US-China Talks
subhead: Saudi Arabia and Iraq lead a nearly 2 million bpd surge in October OPEC crude production; global utilities built a record 21,000 km of transmission lines last year; Beijing's licensing squeeze creates a 125-fold price gap for yttrium ahead of Shenzhen talks; and fusion startups shift focus to superconducting tape.

sections.heading: OPEC Crude Production Rises Nearly 2M Bpd in October as Hormuz Risks Support Prices
sections.body:
OPEC crude oil production surged by nearly 2 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, led by output rebounds in Saudi Arabia (+1.18 million bpd) and Iraq (+496,000 bpd), Anadolu Agency reported on Thursday. Despite the substantial supply addition, global crude benchmarks steadied after earlier declines as ceasefire talks in the Iran conflict made little headway and tanker attacks persisted near the Strait of Hormuz, Bloomberg and Anadolu Agency noted. Speaking at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Qatari Minister of State for International Cooperation Maryam bint Ali Al-Misnad warned that the maritime crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is inflicting increasingly severe damage on global development and energy trade.

Meanwhile, The Times of Israel reported that US Vice President JD Vance is weighing direct talks with senior Iranian officials, even as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told COP31 delegates that US and Israeli strikes on fuel facilities near Asaluyeh and Tehran released roughly 1.5 million tons of carbon dioxide, Bloomberg HT reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi and Iraqi volume increases of nearly 2 million bpd are buffering global physical crude markets against ongoing tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

sections.heading: Global Power Grid Expansion Jumps 50% to Record 21,000 Km as Data Center Demand Soars
sections.body:
Global electric utilities constructed more than 21,000 kilometers of new transmission lines last year—a 50% increase over the prior year and an all-time record, the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) reported at COP31 in Antalya, citing data from the Utilities for Net Zero Alliance via OilPrice. At the same summit, UK Energy Secretary Ed Miliband argued that fossil fuel dependence weakens national security by exposing economies to geopolitical price spikes, while the COP32 Presidency backed Turkey's "35 by 35" initiative to lift electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, Ekonomim reported.

Yet grid additions are still lagging digital demand in North America: The Register reported that US data center electricity requirements are growing 10 times faster than new grid capacity, forcing operators into multi-year connection queues and off-grid generation projects.
sections.whyItMatters: Even a record 50% surge in global transmission line construction is being outpaced tenfold by AI data center load growth in the United States.

sections.heading: Yttrium's 125-Fold Price Gap Looms Over Trump-Xi Summit in Shenzhen
sections.body:
Although Beijing extended its pause on October 2025 rare-earth export controls until January 10, a separate Chinese licensing regime has created a 125-fold price gap between domestic Chinese and international prices for yttrium—a critical mineral essential for high-temperature jet engine coatings, lasers, and superconductors—OilPrice and Reuters reported ahead of next week's expected meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Supply imbalances are also hitting battery and steelmaking materials from the opposite direction: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence warned that persistent global overcapacity in graphite electrodes is driving down margins and raising the risk of further Western plant closures, while North American energy trade faced fresh friction after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared that US-Canada trade talks had collapsed because Washington "asked too much and offered too little," EnergyNow reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing's targeted licensing squeeze on yttrium shows how China can maintain pressure on Western aerospace and energy supply chains even while pausing broader rare-earth export bans.

sections.heading: Private Fusion Investment Hits $14.2B as Race Shifts to Superconducting Tape
sections.body:
Private investors poured a record $4.48 billion into nuclear fusion companies last year—a 69% jump that lifted total private sector funding since 2021 to $14.24 billion, OilPrice reported citing the Fusion Industry Association. With 71% of surveyed fusion developers now targeting commercial power generation before 2035, industry executives say the primary bottleneck has shifted from plasma physics to manufacturing enough high-temperature superconducting tape for reactor magnets.

In fission, the South China Morning Post reported that China now has more than 20 startups developing small modular reactors (SMRs) to compete for global utility contracts alongside state nuclear giants.
sections.whyItMatters: Commercial fusion's transition from laboratory plasma experiments to industrial magnet-tape manufacturing marks a new supply-chain race in advanced nuclear power.

sections.heading: California Refinery Closures Cloud Sable Offshore Revival as Murphy Oil Faces Boycott Calls
sections.body:
In the United States, Sable Offshore's revival of the Santa Ynez oil project off Santa Barbara, California—restarted after a decade of shutdowns following Trump administration intervention—faces a buyer squeeze as California refineries continue to close, OilPrice reported. Meanwhile, North Dakota regulators expect Bakken crude production to hold steady to higher as operators weigh price volatility, EnergyNow noted.

In the Eastern Mediterranean, Houston-based Murphy Oil drew immediate boycott calls from pro-Palestinian groups on Wednesday after stepping in on Monday to replace Eni and Dana Petroleum across six Zone G offshore gas exploration licenses in Israeli waters, OilPrice reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Sable Offshore's dilemma illustrates how state-level downstream refinery closures can strand upstream crude production even when federal regulators clear drilling permits.

bottomLine: Nearly 2 million bpd in added OPEC crude from Saudi Arabia and Iraq is steadying oil prices against Strait of Hormuz attacks, while a 125-fold yttrium price gap and a 10-to-1 ratio between US data center power demand and grid expansion highlight acute physical bottlenecks.
sources: Anadolu Agency, Bloomberg, The Times of Israel, Bloomberg HT, OilPrice, Ekonomim, The Register, Reuters, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, EnergyNow, South China Morning Post
